title: What is A's way out worth?
hook: A could get $0.40 elsewhere; B gets nothing elsewhere. How does the $1 get split?

knows: opportunity cost: what you give up by not taking the next best option
doesNotKnow: that under Nash bargaining each side first gets its outside option and the rest is split equally

misconception: A better outside option only matters if you actually walk away.
objective: The learner can compute a Nash bargaining split (outside options first, the rest halved), finding A $0.70 and B $0.30 when A's option is $0.40 and B's is $0, and explain that the option moves the split without being used.

claims.text: With outside options $0.40 for A and $0 for B, the Nash bargaining split of $1 gives A $0.40 + $0.30 = $0.70 and B $0.30.
claims.source: A = 0.4 + (1 - 0.4 - 0)/2 = 0.70, B = 0.30. Builder's node check (scratchpad ncm-e01-checks/check.mjs): maximising the Nash product (A - 0.4)(B - 0) over A in [0.4, 1] in 0.001 steps gives A = 0.70. Demo.tsx split(). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: maximiser of (A-40)(100-A) over whole cents is A=70; formula 0.4+0.3 = 0.70, B 0.30.

claims.text: The Nash bargaining solution gives each side its outside option plus half of the remaining surplus.
claims.source: J. F. Nash, 'The bargaining problem', Econometrica 18(2), 155-162 (1950); E&K ch. 12 (section unconfirmed). Holds for money-like (linear, transferable) payoffs, as the reveal's model line says. Citation from memory; fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Verified on derivation: with linear payoffs, max (A-a)(B-b) s.t. A+B=1 gives A = a + (1-a-b)/2 (own node for a = 0..80 cents). Nash 1950, Econometrica 18(2) 155-162 correct to my knowledge (not opened). E&K ch. 12 'Bargaining and Power in Networks' confirmed via library-catalogue TOC in web search; section (I believe 12.5) unconfirmed.

claims.text: Every 10 cents added to A's outside option moves 5 cents of the deal to A.
claims.source: With B's option 0, A = a + (1 - a)/2 = 0.5 + a/2, so dA/da = 1/2. Builder's node table: a = 0, 0.1, ..., 1 gives A = 0.50, 0.55, ..., 1.00. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): A = 0.5 + a/2: own node table a = 0..80 gives 50, 55, ..., 90 cents.

claims.text: In the model the deal always happens, so A never takes the outside option; the option only moves the split.
claims.source: For any a < 1, the deal gives A = 0.5 + a/2 > a and B = (1 - a)/2 > 0, so both prefer the deal to no deal. Model assumption: the agreement is reached. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): For a < 1, A = 0.5 + a/2 > a and B = (1-a)/2 > 0 (own node, all slider values). Model assumption stated.

claims.text: The stage is a model: money payoffs, both sides value a dollar the same, and the deal is sure to happen.
claims.source: Modelling choice stated in the reveal. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Matches the reveal's muted model line.

claims.text: Moving A's outside option from one value to another moves A's deal by half the change: for example from $0.40 to $0.80 (40 cents) takes A's deal from $0.70 to $0.90 (20 cents). (Stage: the 'Tried (option → A gets)' row lists every option set; the reveal quotes its lowest and highest entries.)
claims.source: A = a + (1 - a)/2 = 1/2 + a/2 with B's option 0, so dA = da/2. Demo.tsx v2 reveal computes the learner's last change from split(prev) and split(a); the dashed 'before' line marks split(prev).A. Builder, 2026-10-14. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. A = a + (100 - a)/2, so dA = da/2. Own node over every reachable option (0..80 step 10): 70 -> 85, 80 -> 90; all whole cents. Reveal computes from split(prev) and split(a). | Builder revision v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): (r7) The reveal no longer quotes the last slider stop (a two-press slider move passed $0.70 in a blink); it quotes the lowest and highest options in the persistent Tried row, lo -> hi, and split(lo).A -> split(hi).A. A = a + (100 - a)/2 cents, so the change in A is (hi - lo)/2 for any pair. Title and hook rewritten so they no longer say A never walks away (that ruled out the $0.40 option before the commit). Builder statement, not self-verified.

recall.question: Two people split $1 by Nash bargaining. A can get $0.60 elsewhere, B nothing. What does A get?
recall.why: A first gets the $0.60 fallback; the remaining $0.40 is split evenly, so A gets $0.80 without ever taking the outside offer.
